yawes.c: YAWES. At Sea, they fay a Ship makes Yawes, When thro ’ the fault of him at Helm slie is not kept steady in her Course, but makes Angles in and out; to prevent which, the Conner crys, steady, steady, keep her Thus, Thus.

year.c: YEAR: The Time the Sun takes to go through the twelve Signs of the Zodiack. This is properly the Natural or Tropical Year, and contains Days, Hour, and Minutes. The ydereal Year, in that Time in Which the Sun departing from any fixed Star, comes to it a - gain; and this is in Days, Hours, and almost x o Minutes. But according to Sir Isaac Newtons, New Theory of the Moon, the Sydereft Year is D. H. ' "; and the Tropical, D. H. ' ". The Civil Tear, which is commonly used by all Nations, is very various, both as to its Beginning, and also as to its Length, according as they follow the Course of the Sun, Moon, or both. ? The Civil Lunar Year contains Lunations of Synodical Months, aud contains but Days: This being Days less than the Solar Year, its Head in about Years will run through all the Months and Seasons of the Year. This kind of Year is now used by the Turks, and seems to have had its first Rife in Countries where the difference between Summer and Winter is not so sensible as it is with us; and where for want of Astronomy ) they know not how to estimate the Solar Year, and therefore began their Account Of Months from the Phases of the Moon. And hence, as the learn - ed Aftronomef Dr. Gregory hints, it came to pass that they began the Account of their Civil Day at Sun - fet for their Day must begin when their Month and Year did, and that Was, with the New Moon, which being to be determind by view, could not be discover ’ d till after Sun - fet. The Jews had their Secular Year, Which began at the Autumnal Equinox; and their Sacred Tear Which began at the Vernal one. The Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Affyrians, first measured the Year, by the Course of the Sun which they fuppdsd to contain but Days afterwards more were added by Mercury, which he called imyoptStfets, i. e. added; but yet no notice was taken of the Hours, by which means, the Egyptian Year hath fixed no Place in reference to the true Solar Year; but anticipating a Day every four Years, runs quite round in Years. This Way of reckoning continued till Egypt be - coming a Province of the Roman Empire, they took the Julian Account, only they kept the Names of their Months still, and ordered their matter so, that their That, the first Day of the Year, always happen ’ d on the th of August in the Julian Year., So that the Egyptian or Coptic k. Year is Months and Days before the Roman Year, Which begins with the Calends of January. The Perftans Account ( according to the Egyptian way ) Days. The Arabs, Saracens, and Turkj, count their Year by the motion of the Moon, and make it con - fist of Moons or Months, whereof feme have, and feme Days alternately; and these al - together make but Days; so that their Month Muharran, in which they place the beginning of the Year, in less than Years Will run quite round, and be in all Seasons. The Arabs indeed, by a Cycle of Years, do remedy this, by means of an Intercalation or Embolism of Days. The Greeks counted their Year by the motion of both Sun and Moon, and finding that there was Days difference between the Lunar and Solar Year; at first they added an Intercalary Month every two Years, containing Days, which there - fore they Called ept. tipt. dJov, the added or inserted Month. Afterwards considering the Hours also, they put their Embolism off till Years end; and then making the first Years to contain Days apiece, ( which is the Lunar Year ) this made the th Year to have Days. And to make this In - tercalation the more Remarkable, they instituted the Olympic Games, on every such th Year whence came the Computation by Olympiads; each of which contained Years. Nevertheless they found that this would not do ) in process of Time; and therefore they first red - ced the Intercalation to and then to Years but still there was great Confusion, till one Meto, a Citizen and famous Astronomer of Athens j thought of joining the two last Periods and i together together; which doing, he made a Period of Years, in which the two motions of the Sun and Moon are wholly accommodated, and the Moon changes on the fame Day of the Month that she did Years before. This Discovery, for its Ful - ness, was much Celebrated, and the Number of the Period, the Athenians ordered to be let up in a publick place, and to be written in Characters of Gold; whence it took the Name it still retains, being called the Golden Number. The Athenians began their Year at the New Moon after the Summer Solstice j in their Mouth Hecatonibaon, as Plutarch says. There were also some Nations who made their. Year to consist only of, or of but Months, as Macrobius tells us in his Saturnalia, Lib,. The Carians and Acharnanians, faith Just In, made their Year to consist of Months, and reckoned but Dayi to their Month. The Romans had three forts of Years: r. That of Romulus, which contained but ten Months; from whence the last Month of our Year retains the Name of December, as being the Tenth of his. This Year begun in March.. Numa Pompilius his Year; which had Romulus his gross Mistake corrected, and two more Months added to it, vi, January and February; and then it contained only Days, dr Lunar Months.. The Year of Julius Cafar, who discovering that there were Days more than Numa reckon ’ d, made the Year Days: And reserving the Hours till every fourth Year, they then made another Day, which was added before the sixth of the Calends of March; so that in this fourth Year they accounted the th of the Calends of March twice Bis - sexto - calendas, whence came the Word Bifftextile or Leap - Year, as we call it; which hath Days. This Account is now used in England, and is the Julian or Old Stile. But because there was still found an Error in this Calculation, and that the Equinoxes did plainly, ' f tho ’ insensibly recede from the Points where Cafar had fix d them; as also, that the Year was dise - ver ’ d to want about i Minutes of Days and Hours - which Minutes will in Years make the Equinoxes go back about a Day; Pops Gregory X III. to Reform ( as he thought ) this Error, ' ordered to Days to be taken from the Year, to bring the Equinoxes that Year ( which was S J ) to March, and Sept.,. And this is what is called the Gregorian Account or New Stile, as is used by the Popish Nations every where. The Great Tear, or the Annus Magnus, about or Years; in which Time the Fix ’ d Stars will appear to come to the fame Point again,. exaCtly after one entire Revolution. ?

yearandday.c: YEAR and Day, in Law, is a Time that deter - mines a Right in many Cafes; and in some Works an Usucaption, in others a Prescription; as in case of an Estray, if the Owner ( ' Proclamations being made ) challenge it not within that Time, it is For - set: So is the Tear and Day given in case of Ap - peal, in case of Descent after Entry or Claim, and in case of a Man so Bruised and Wounded; of ProreCtion, Essoigns in respects the King ’ s Service j of a Wreck, and divers other Cafes. yearday.c: YEAR, Day and baste, is a part of the King Prerogative, whereby he Chailengeth the Profits of their Lands and Tenements for a Year and a Day, that are Attainted of Petty Treason, or Felony ! whoever is Lord of the Mannor whereto the Lands or Tenements belong; and not only so, but in the end may waste the Tenements, destroy the Houses, ' root up the Woods, Gardens, Pasture, and plow up the Meadows, except the Lord of the Soil agree with him for Redemption of such VaJlel after - ' wards restoring it to the Lord of the Fee.

yard.c: YARD - LAND, Virgata Terra, is a Quantity of Land, various according to the Place: At Wimblcton in Surrey ’ tis accounted sis - teen Acres in other Counties ’ tis twenty; in stone twenty four, in some thirty, and in others even four Acres. In a M. S. of the Abbacy of Malmesbury, a Virgate of Land is said to contain twenty four Acres. This uncertain Quantity in '. E. i. is called a Verge of Land.
